blocks.text: 1. Decision Trees

blocks.alt: A root node branches down into a leaf that holds the prediction

blocks.text: Logistic Regression, KNN, Naive Bayes, and SVM all reason about classification in continuous terms, whether that means a linear score, a distance measurement, a probability product, or a geometric margin. Decision Trees abandon that continuous machinery entirely in favor of something closer to how a person might actually reason through a decision: a sequence of simple yes or no questions, each one narrowing down the possibilities until a final answer is reached.

This is directly the same algorithm already introduced as Decision Tree Regression in the Regression module, just aimed at a different kind of target. Where Decision Tree Regression split the data to minimize the spread of a continuous numeric target within each resulting group, Decision Tree Classification splits the data to make each resulting group as pure as possible in terms of class labels. The recursive splitting mechanics are identical between the two; only the measure of what makes a good split changes.
2. The Structure of a Tree

A decision tree begins at a single root node holding the entire training dataset. At the root, and at every subsequent internal node, the tree asks one feature-based question, is income above 50000, is credit score above 700, and routes each training example down the yes branch or the no branch depending on its answer. This process repeats recursively at each resulting child node, asking a new question and splitting further, until the tree reaches a leaf node, at which point it stops and simply predicts whichever class is most common among the training examples that landed there.

A trained tree can be read directly as a nested set of if-else rules, and predicting a new example is simply a matter of walking down from the root, answering each question along the way based on that example's feature values, until arriving at a leaf and returning its predicted class.
3. How Splits Are Chosen

blocks.alt: A candidate split gets chosen for the best impurity reduction

blocks.text: The central algorithmic question in building a decision tree is: at any given node, which feature should be tested, and at what threshold. The standard approach is exhaustive and greedy. At each node, the algorithm considers every available feature and, for continuous features, every possible threshold value that could split the data, evaluating how good each candidate split would be.

Goodness of a split is measured by how much purer the two resulting child groups become compared to the parent node, using an impurity measure covered in the next section. The single best split, the one producing the largest improvement, is chosen, the data is divided accordingly into two child nodes, and the entire process repeats independently inside each child. This greedy, recursive procedure, choosing the locally best split at every single step without looking ahead, is what actually builds the tree from the root downward.
4. Measuring Impurity

blocks.alt: A pure node with one class has low impurity while a mixed node has high impurity

blocks.text: A node is called pure if every training example that landed there belongs to the same class; its impurity is zero. A node is impure if it contains a mix of classes, and the more evenly mixed that node is, the higher its impurity. Two standard measures quantify this. Gini Impurity computes the probability that two examples picked at random from the node, with replacement, would belong to different classes; it ranges from 0 for a pure node up to a maximum that depends on the number of classes.

Entropy, borrowed directly from information theory, measures the average amount of information needed to correctly identify the class of a randomly chosen example from the node; a pure node needs zero information since the answer is already certain, while a perfectly balanced mix of classes needs the maximum. Both measures capture essentially the same underlying idea, how mixed the classes are within a node, and in practice they tend to produce very similar trees; Gini is the scikit-learn default primarily because it is slightly cheaper to compute, avoiding a logarithm.

blocks.text: 5. Information Gain

blocks.alt: Impurity before the split and impurity after the split together produce information gain

blocks.text: Choosing the best split at any node requires comparing candidate splits directly, and Information Gain is the standard way to do that. It is computed as the impurity of the parent node before splitting, minus the weighted average impurity of the two child nodes after splitting, where the weights are proportional to how many training examples end up in each child. A larger Information Gain means the split did more to separate the classes into purer groups.

The tree-building algorithm evaluates Information Gain for every candidate feature and threshold at each node and greedily selects whichever single split maximizes it. This greedy, one-step-at-a-time selection is efficient but not globally optimal, since a slightly worse split now could in principle enable much better splits later; finding the globally optimal tree is computationally intractable for any real-sized dataset, so every practical decision tree implementation relies on this greedy approximation.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Information Gain computed with Entropy is sometimes specifically called the ID3 or C4.5 criterion, named after early decision tree algorithms. Gini-based splitting is sometimes called the CART criterion, for Classification And Regression Trees, the same family scikit-learn implements for both this topic and Decision Tree Regression.

blocks.text: 6. Same Algorithm, Different Criterion

It is worth being explicit about just how much Decision Tree Classification shares with Decision Tree Regression, covered earlier in the Regression module. Both build a tree through the exact same recursive, greedy splitting procedure, and both use max_depth, min_samples_split, and similar controls to manage complexity. The only real difference between them is the criterion used to score a candidate split: Decision Tree Regression minimizes the variance, or spread, of the numeric target within each resulting group, while Decision Tree Classification minimizes Gini Impurity or Entropy, measuring the mix of class labels instead.

This shared foundation is why scikit-learn implements both as DecisionTreeRegressor and DecisionTreeClassifier from the same underlying CART, Classification And Regression Trees, family, and it is also why every ensemble method built on top of decision trees, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and the rest, transfers so directly between regression and classification tasks: swap the splitting criterion and the leaf prediction rule, and the rest of the machinery carries over unchanged.
7. The Overfitting Problem

blocks.alt: A very deep tree ends up memorizing the training data

blocks.text: A decision tree allowed to grow without any restriction will keep splitting nodes until every single leaf is perfectly pure, meaning every leaf contains examples from only one class. In the extreme, this can mean leaves containing just one or two training examples each, effectively memorizing individual training rows rather than learning a general pattern that would transfer to new data. This is a severe and very common form of overfitting, and it is the single most important practical issue to manage when training decision trees.

An unrestricted, fully grown tree will typically show excellent, even perfect, accuracy on its own training data while performing noticeably worse on a held-out validation or test set, a clear symptom of high variance, the same overfitting concept first framed back in Ridge Regression and revisited throughout the Regression module. Controlling this tendency is essential to getting a decision tree that actually generalizes.
8. Controlling Tree Complexity

blocks.alt: Max depth and min samples per leaf together control tree size

blocks.text: Several hyperparameters directly control how large and complex a decision tree is allowed to grow, and tuning them is the primary defense against overfitting. max_depth caps how many levels of splits the tree can have, directly limiting how complex any single decision path can become. min_samples_split requires a node to contain at least a certain number of training examples before it is even allowed to be split further, preventing splits based on tiny, unreliable subsets of data. min_samples_leaf enforces a similar minimum on every resulting leaf, preventing the tree from carving out leaves that represent just one or two examples.

An alternative strategy is pruning: first grow a full, unrestricted tree, then trim back branches that do not meaningfully improve performance on a held-out validation set, working from the leaves back toward the root. Cost-complexity pruning, available in scikit-learn through the ccp_alpha parameter, formalizes this by penalizing tree complexity directly during the pruning decision. In practice, tuning max_depth and min_samples_leaf via cross-validation is the more commonly used approach, since it is simpler to reason about and computationally cheaper than full post-growth pruning.

blocks.title: tip
blocks.content: There is no universally correct value for these hyperparameters; the right setting depends on dataset size and noise level. Cross-validation, covered in its own module later in this course, is the standard way to choose them rather than guessing a fixed number.

blocks.text: 9. Interpretability as a Practical Advantage

blocks.alt: A decision tree is easy to explain

blocks.text: Beyond its predictive mechanics, a decision tree offers something none of the previous classifiers in this module provide directly: a fully transparent, human-readable explanation for every single prediction. Tracing the exact sequence of yes or no questions from the root down to the leaf that produced a given prediction yields a plain-language rule, something like if income is above 50000 and credit score is above 700, then approve the loan.

This stands in sharp contrast to Logistic Regression, whose explanation lives in coefficients and log-odds, SVM, whose explanation lives in a geometric margin in a possibly kernel-transformed space, or Naive Bayes, whose explanation lives in a product of probabilities. In regulated domains like lending or medical diagnosis, where a model’s decisions may need to be explained to a regulator, an auditor, or the affected individual, this direct interpretability is often as important as raw predictive accuracy, and it is one of the main reasons decision trees remain in active use even though the ensemble methods covered later in this module usually outperform a single tree on accuracy.
10. Worked Example
The example below fits a shallow, depth-limited decision tree classifier and prints the resulting rules in plain text, showing exactly how a prediction traces back through the tree.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Features: income (thousands), credit score. Label: loan approved (1) or not (0)
X = np.array([[30, 600], [45, 650], [60, 700], [80, 750], [25, 580],
              [90, 780], [35, 620], [70, 720], [50, 660], [20, 550]])
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

model = DecisionTreeClassifier(
    criterion='gini',
    max_depth=3,
    min_samples_leaf=2,
    random_state=42
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

predictions = model.predict(X_test)
print("Accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_test, predictions))
print("Feature importances:", model.feature_importances_)

# Print the tree as a set of readable rules
tree_rules = export_text(model, feature_names=['income', 'credit_score'])
print(tree_rules)

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: export_text prints the tree exactly as a nested set of if-else rules, feature by feature and threshold by threshold, matching the plain-language decision path described conceptually throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Decision Trees classify by asking a sequence of simple yes/no feature questions, routing examples down to a leaf prediction.
Splits are chosen greedily at each node by testing every feature and threshold and picking the one maximizing Information Gain.
Gini Impurity and Entropy both measure how mixed the classes are within a node; Gini is the faster, more common default.
Decision Tree Classification shares its entire splitting algorithm with Decision Tree Regression, differing only in the impurity criterion used.
An unrestricted tree overfits severely, growing until every leaf is perfectly pure and memorizing training noise.
max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, and pruning all control tree complexity and fight overfitting.
A trained tree is fully interpretable: any prediction traces back to a plain-language chain of feature rules.
A single tree usually underperforms the ensemble methods covered next, but its transparency remains a real practical advantage.
Next up: Random Forest, which combines many decision trees together to trade away some interpretability for substantially better accuracy.
